text: Blackwood's column arrived at dawn, exactly as disciplined and unhurried as her reputation promised, moving through Sherwood's approaches with a caution that spoke to every hard lesson Ashcombe had cost her — no overconfidence this time, no assumptions about an easy victory, simply patient, methodical pressure applied precisely where the terrain allowed her the greatest advantage.
“She's learned,” Marian observed, watching the formation from their own carefully prepared position. “No obvious weaknesses to exploit this time. She's not making the same mistakes twice.”

“Then we don't rely on her mistakes,” Robin said, steady, watching his father check his borrowed sword with the particular grim focus of a man determined not to let unfamiliarity become a liability. “We rely on everything else we've actually got.”

The fighting, when it broke, carried none of the loose comic chaos that had once defined this crew's earliest, luckier encounters — this was hard, disciplined defense, every position held with real purpose, every advantage Marian's careful planning had identified actually put to proper use.

Edmund fought with the particular fierce, unpolished determination of a man discovering, considerably later in life than he'd expected to, that old training half-forgotten could still serve when it genuinely mattered — clumsy in places, but never once hesitant, protecting the position assigned to him with a ferocity that surprised even himself.
“You're rather better at this than you let on,” Long John called, impressed, ducking a soldier's blade nearby.
“I'm considerably more motivated than I look,” Edmund called back, and found, despite everything, that he meant it entirely.

text: The crew fought as they'd learned to fight across a long, difficult year — not perfectly, never perfectly, but with the particular hard-won coordination of people who had survived enough genuine danger together to trust each other completely when it mattered most. Marian directed the defense with brisk, unerring precision. Will and Thistlewood worked the flanks with careful, deniable efficiency. Pip moved through the chaos with an ease that spoke to considerably more training than her slight frame suggested.

Blackwood's soldiers, disciplined as they were, found themselves facing a defense considerably more coordinated than their own careful planning had accounted for — ground given grudgingly, positions held with a stubbornness that began, slowly but unmistakably, to shift the battle's actual momentum.
“She's losing ground,” Robin said, watching the formation waver. “Properly losing it, this time.”

It was in the confusion of that shifting momentum that Blackwood herself finally broke through toward the position Edmund held, exactly as her orders had always intended — patient, controlled, entirely focused on the single objective that had brought her army this far.
“Edmund of Loxby,” she said, sword raised, unhurried even now. “You'll come with me, and this ends considerably more gently for everyone else here than it otherwise might.”
Robin was there before she'd finished speaking, placing himself directly between his father and her blade with fierce, immediate resolve. “You'll have to go through me first.”
“I rather expected I might,” Blackwood said, and something in her voice, for the first time since her arrival, carried the smallest crack of genuine uncertainty.

sequence._describe: Robin of Loxby and Edmund facing Captain Blackwood directly, swords raised, tense personal standoff, Blackwood's composure beginning to crack. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, tense dramatic daytime lighting, high-stakes emotional mood.

text: “I've fought you before,” Robin said, steady despite the danger, sword raised between his father and hers. “I've fought considerably worse than you before, honestly, and I'm rather done losing people I care about to men and women simply following orders they've never properly questioned.”

“I don't have the luxury of questioning orders,” Blackwood said, though something in how she said it carried considerably less conviction than her usual professional certainty. “I serve the Sheriff. That service doesn't generally permit the kind of sentiment you're describing.”

“Doesn't it?” Edmund asked, quiet, stepping forward despite Robin's protective stance, meeting her eyes directly. “You're an intelligent woman, Captain. You've had weeks to study my family. You know precisely what you're being asked to break, dragging me away from them now. I'd ask you, soldier to soldier in whatever sense either of us still qualifies, whether that's actually a service you can live with providing.”

Blackwood was quiet a long moment, sword still raised, something working behind her carefully controlled features that Robin had genuinely never witnessed from her before — not weakness, exactly, but the particular difficult stillness of a disciplined woman confronting a line she hadn't fully realized, until this precise moment, that she'd actually reached.

“I fought for considerably worthier causes than this, once,” she said, finally, quiet. “Before the Sheriff's coin made the question of worthiness rather less relevant to my daily calculations. I find I'd forgotten, rather thoroughly, what it actually felt like to be asked to do something my own conscience couldn't properly defend.”

“Then don't,” Marian said, arriving at Robin's side, steady and direct. “Whatever coin the Sheriff's paying you, it's not worth becoming a woman who tears families apart for a living. You've shown more honor than that, every time we've faced you.”

sequence._describe: Captain Blackwood lowering her sword and calling for retreat, her soldiers withdrawing in disciplined order, a genuine personal choice visible in her bearing. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. text: Blackwood lowered her sword, slowly, something old and tired and finally, genuinely resolved settling across her disciplined features.
“Fall back,” she called, to her scattered soldiers, clear and carrying despite the chaos still surrounding them. “All of you. We're finished here.”
“Captain—” one of her lieutenants started, confused, gesturing toward the battle's still-uncertain shape.

“I said fall back,” Blackwood repeated, sharper now, entirely certain despite the visible cost the decision carried. “This particular fight isn't one I intend to finish. Whatever the Sheriff makes of that decision, he can make of it directly to my face, rather than through the blood of a family that's done nothing worse than finally find each other again.”

Her soldiers withdrew in the same disciplined order that had defined their arrival, no rout, no panic, simply a controlled retreat carrying, this time, the unmistakable weight of a genuine, personal choice rather than mere tactical calculation.
Blackwood herself lingered a moment longer, meeting Robin's gaze, then Edmund's, with something that finally, unmistakably resembled real respect rather than professional assessment.

“I don't know what becomes of my position, after today,” she said. “The Sheriff doesn't generally forgive failures this costly to his own designs. But I find, having finally reached this particular line, that I'd rather face whatever comes of standing on the right side of it than continue serving whatever I'd have had to become to cross it.” She turned to follow her retreating soldiers, pausing only once more. “Take care of each other. Whatever else changes, I find I rather hope you manage that much.”

text: The battlefield settled slowly into exhausted, disbelieving quiet, the whole crew gathering close around Edmund with the particular fierce relief of people who had genuinely, properly won something that had felt, only hours before, considerably less certain.

“You did well,” Robin said to his father, real pride plain in his voice, checking him over for injury with careful, protective attention. “Better than well. I don't think I properly understood, until today, what kind of man you actually are, underneath everything that kept us apart.”

“I had rather excellent motivation,” Edmund said, echoing his own earlier words, though something genuine and moved worked beneath the small joke. “And rather remarkable people showing me exactly what fighting for family properly looks like.”

Marian, watching the retreat's dust finally settle on the horizon, found herself turning the whole shape of the victory over with her usual careful attention, unable to fully set aside the awareness of what still remained.

“Blackwood's done, I think,” she said, quiet, to Robin. “Genuinely done, this time — not simply retreated to return more carefully, but actually finished with this particular fight. That's no small thing.”

“No,” Robin agreed, watching the horizon with her, something complicated working behind his own hard-won relief. “But the Sheriff's still out there. Whatever Blackwood's choice costs her, it won't stop him from eventually sending someone else, or coming himself, once he's finished being furious about today's failure.”

“I know,” Marian said, quiet. “But that's a fight for another day. Today, we won. Today, your father's safe, and this family's still whole.” She looked around at the exhausted, relieved, thoroughly victorious group surrounding them. “I find that's rather worth simply sitting with, for now, before we start properly worrying about tomorrow.”
